questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The current in a conductor varies with time as I = (2 + 4t) A, where t is in seconds. The charge that flows through any cross-section of the conductor between t = 0 and t = 3 s is:

solution.concept: Current is the rate of flow of charge: q = ∫I dt (area under the I–t graph)
solution.explanation: When the current changes with time, the charge is the area under the current–time graph, not the final current multiplied by the time.
solution.shortcut: I rises linearly from 2 A to 14 A, so the average current is 8 A and q = 8 × 3 = 24 C.
solution.why_others_wrong: 42 C multiplies the final current (14 A) by the whole time. 36 C integrates 4t as 4t² instead of 2t² and leaves out the constant part. 6 C keeps only the constant 2 A part.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electric current

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Three resistors, each of 6 Ω, are connected to form a triangle. The equivalent resistance between any two corners of the triangle is:

solution.concept: Series and parallel combination
solution.explanation: Between two corners, one resistor connects them directly and the other two form a 12 Ω series path; these two paths are in parallel.
steps: Direct path: 6 Ω; other path: 6 + 6 = 12 Ω
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 Ω puts all three resistors in series. 2 Ω puts all three in parallel. 3 Ω takes the two paths as 6 Ω each.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors - series and parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When resistors are connected in series across a battery, the same current flows through each of them.
Statement II: When resistors are connected in parallel across a battery, the potential difference across each resistor is inversely proportional to its resistance.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Series: common current; parallel: common potential difference
solution.explanation: In a series connection there is only one path, so the current is the same in every resistor (Statement I true). In a parallel connection every resistor is connected between the same two points, so the potential difference is the same across each; it is the current that is inversely proportional to the resistance (Statement II false).
steps: Series: I same in all → I true
Parallel: V same across all; I ∝ 1/R → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II confuses the current (which divides inversely as R) with the potential difference (which is common to all the resistors).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors - series and parallel
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The current–voltage (I–V) graphs of the same metal wire, taken at two different temperatures T₁ and T₂, are straight lines through the origin, the line for T₁ being steeper (larger slope, I plotted against V) than the line for T₂. It follows that:

options.text: T₁ is higher than T₂, because a steeper I–V line means a larger resistance
T₁ is equal to T₂, because the slope of an I–V graph does not depend on temperature
T₁ is higher than T₂, because the resistivity of a metal decreases as its temperature rises
T₁ is lower than T₂, because the wire has a smaller resistance at T₁

solution.concept: Slope of the I–V graph = 1/R; the resistance of a metal increases with temperature
solution.explanation: For an I–V graph, the slope is I/V = 1/R. A steeper line means a smaller resistance. The resistance of a metal wire increases with temperature, so the smaller resistance belongs to the lower temperature.
steps: Slope of I–V line = 1/R → line for T₁ has the smaller R
R of a metal rises with temperature → T₁ < T₂
solution.why_others_wrong: A steeper I–V line means a smaller, not larger, resistance. The slope does depend on temperature because R does. The resistivity of a metal increases, not decreases, with temperature.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', temperature dependence of resistivity
solution.final_answer: Option D: T₁ is lower than T₂, because the wire has a smaller resistance at T₁

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: While applying Kirchhoff's loop rule, when a resistor R is traversed in the direction of the current I through it, the change in potential is −IR.
Statement II: While applying Kirchhoff's loop rule, when an ideal cell of emf ε is traversed from its negative terminal to its positive terminal, the change in potential is +ε.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Sign conventions of the loop rule
solution.explanation: Current flows through a resistor from higher to lower potential, so going along the current the potential falls by IR (Statement I true). The positive terminal of a cell is at a potential ε higher than its negative terminal, so going from − to + the potential rises by ε (Statement II true).
steps: Along the current in R: potential drops by IR → change −IR → I true
Ideal cell, − to +: potential rises by ε → change +ε → II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both sign conventions are correct, so the options that call either statement false are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Kirchhoff's rules
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Battery X (emf 12 V, internal resistance 2 Ω) and battery Y (emf 6 V, internal resistance 2 Ω) are connected in parallel, positive terminal to positive terminal and negative terminal to negative terminal, and a 4 Ω resistor is connected across the combination. The current through battery Y is:

options.text: 0.6 A, flowing out of its positive terminal
1.5 A, flowing out of its positive terminal
0.6 A, flowing into its positive terminal (Y is being charged)
1.8 A, flowing out of its positive terminal

solution.concept: Kirchhoff's junction rule at the common positive terminal
solution.explanation: Let V be the potential of the common positive line (negative line at 0 V). The currents leaving the line through the two batteries' internal resistances and the 4 Ω resistor must add to zero.
steps: Current through Y = (7.2 − 6)/2 = 0.6 A, from the positive line into Y's positive terminal
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.6 A out of the positive terminal has the right size but the wrong direction: the common terminal voltage (7.2 V) exceeds Y's emf, so Y is charged. 1.5 A treats Y as if it alone fed the 4 Ω resistor. 1.8 A is the current in the 4 Ω resistor.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Kirchhoff's rules
solution.final_answer: Option C: 0.6 A, flowing into its positive terminal (Y is being charged)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A coil of wire is placed in the left gap of a metre bridge and a standard 10.0 Ω resistor in the right gap. With the coil at 20 °C, the null point is 50.0 cm from the left end of the wire. The coil alone is then heated to 120 °C (the standard resistor stays at 20 °C), and the null point moves to 60.0 cm from the left end. Taking the temperature coefficient of resistance of the coil's material as constant and referred to 20 °C, its value is:

solution.concept: Metre bridge balance X/R = l/(100 − l) combined with R_T = R₂₀[1 + α(T − 20)]
solution.explanation: At 20 °C the null point is at the middle, so the coil has 10.0 Ω. At 120 °C the balance gives the hot resistance, and the fractional increase divided by the temperature rise is α.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.5 × 10⁻² °C⁻¹ divides the ratio R_T/R₂₀ (not the fractional increase) by ΔT. 3.3 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹ divides the increase by the hot resistance instead of the resistance at 20 °C. 2.0 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹ uses 60/50 instead of 60/40 for the balance ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Wheatstone bridge; temperature dependence of resistivity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A copper wire of cross-sectional area 1.0 mm² is joined end to end with an aluminium wire of cross-sectional area 2.0 mm², and a steady current flows through the two wires in series. The number densities of free electrons are 8.0 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ in copper and 6.0 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ in aluminium. The ratio of the drift speed of the electrons in the copper wire to that in the aluminium wire is:

solution.concept: I = neAv_d with the same current in both wires
solution.explanation: In series the current is the same, so n A v_d is the same in both wires and v_d ∝ 1/(nA).
steps: n_Cu A_Cu v_Cu = n_Al A_Al v_Al
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.67 inverts the ratio. 2.0 uses the areas alone and ignores the electron densities. 0.75 uses the electron densities alone and ignores the areas.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The resistance of the tungsten filament of an electric bulb is much larger when the bulb is glowing than when it is cold.
Reason (R): The resistivity of a metal increases as its temperature rises.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Temperature dependence of the resistivity of metals
solution.explanation: A glowing filament is at a very high temperature (well above 2000 °C). Since the resistivity of a metal rises with temperature, the hot filament has a much higher resistance than the cold one. R gives exactly this reason.
steps: ρ of a metal increases with T → R = ρl/A increases
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and the rise of resistivity with temperature is the cause of the larger hot resistance, so R correctly explains A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', temperature dependence of resistivity
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A cell of emf 12 V and internal resistance 1 Ω is connected across an external resistor of 5 Ω. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The current in the circuit is 2 A.
(b) The potential difference between the terminals of the cell is 10 V.
(c) The power dissipated in the 5 Ω resistor is 24 W.
(d) The power dissipated inside the cell is 4 W.
(e) If the 5 Ω resistor is replaced by a wire of negligible resistance, the current becomes 6 A.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: I = ε/(R + r), V = ε − Ir, P = I²R
solution.explanation: I = 12/(5 + 1) = 2 A (a true). V = 12 − 2 × 1 = 10 V (b true). Power in the 5 Ω resistor = 2² × 5 = 20 W, not 24 W; 24 W is the total power εI (c false). Power inside the cell = 2² × 1 = 4 W (d true). With R = 0, the current is ε/r = 12 A, not 6 A (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (c) or (e) include a false statement; (a) and (d) only leaves out the true statement (b).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance; electrical power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each material in List-I with its approximate resistivity at room temperature in List-II, as tabulated in NCERT.

List-I:
A. Copper
B. Nichrome
C. Germanium
D. Glass

List-II:
I. 10¹⁰ to 10¹⁴ Ω m
II. 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m
III. 0.46 Ω m
IV. about 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Resistivities of metals, alloys, semiconductors and insulators
solution.explanation: Metals such as copper have the lowest resistivities (about 10⁻⁸ Ω m). Alloys such as nichrome are about a hundred times more resistive (about 10⁻⁶ Ω m). Semiconductors such as germanium lie in between (0.46 Ω m), and insulators such as glass have enormous resistivities (10¹⁰–10¹⁴ Ω m).
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV, B-II swaps the metal and the alloy. B-III, C-IV gives the alloy a semiconductor's resistivity. C-I, D-III swaps the semiconductor and the insulator.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', resistivity of various materials (table)
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A 4 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor are connected to an ideal 12 V battery, first in series with each other and then in parallel with each other. Match each case in List-I with the power dissipated in List-II.

List-I:
A. Power in the 4 Ω resistor, series connection
B. Power in the 12 Ω resistor, series connection
C. Power in the 4 Ω resistor, parallel connection
D. Power in the 12 Ω resistor, parallel connection

List-II:
I. 12 W
II. 2.25 W
III. 36 W
IV. 6.75 W

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Series: same current, P = I²R; parallel: same voltage, P = V²/R
solution.explanation: In series the current is 12/16 = 0.75 A in both, so the larger resistor takes more power. In parallel each resistor has the full 12 V, so the smaller resistor takes more power.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV, B-II gives the smaller resistor more power in series. C-I, D-III gives the larger resistor more power in parallel. A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV swaps the series and parallel results.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electrical power; combination of resistors
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An infinitely long ladder network is made of identical 2 Ω resistors. Each section of the ladder has one 2 Ω resistor along the upper line followed by one 2 Ω resistor connected across from the upper line to the lower line; the lower line has no resistance. The equivalent resistance between the two input terminals of the ladder is:

solution.concept: Self-similarity of an infinite ladder: removing the first section leaves the same ladder
solution.explanation: Let the input resistance be x. The first series 2 Ω resistor is followed by the first rung (2 Ω) in parallel with the rest of the ladder, whose resistance is again x.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2(1 + √3) Ω is the result for a ladder with a series resistor on both lines in every section. 4 Ω keeps only the first section (2 + 2). An infinite number of resistors does not give infinite resistance, because the later sections are in parallel with the rungs.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A voltmeter of resistance 200 Ω, connected directly across the terminals of a cell, reads 1.20 V. When it is replaced by a voltmeter of resistance 450 Ω, the reading is 1.35 V. Nothing else is connected to the cell. The emf and the internal resistance of the cell are:

solution.concept: A voltmeter of finite resistance draws current, so it reads the terminal voltage V = ε − Ir
solution.explanation: Each voltmeter is the only load, so the current through the cell is the voltmeter reading divided by the voltmeter's resistance. Two readings give two equations for ε and r.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.35 V and zero treats the 450 Ω voltmeter as ideal. 1.2 V and 50 Ω takes the first reading as the emf. 1.5 V and 0.02 Ω inverts the ratio when finding r (ΔI/ΔV instead of ΔV/ΔI).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The current density in a long straight wire of radius 1.0 mm is directed along the wire, and its magnitude increases linearly with the distance r from the axis: J = kr, with k = 3.0 × 10⁸ A m⁻³. The current in the wire is about:

solution.concept: Current is the flux of current density: I = ∫J dA
solution.explanation: Since J varies with r, divide the cross-section into thin rings of radius r and width dr (area 2πr dr) and add their currents.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.94 A multiplies the surface value kR by the whole area. 0.47 A uses the value of J at r = R/2 as the average. 1.9 A leaves out the factor 1/3 from the integration.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electric current; current density

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
In a Wheatstone bridge, P = 10 Ω (from A to B) and Q = 20 Ω (from B to C) form one arm, and R = 30 Ω (from A to D) and S = 60 Ω (from D to C) form the other. An ideal 9 V battery is connected between A (positive) and C, and a galvanometer between B and D. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The bridge is balanced, and no current flows through the galvanometer.
(b) The current through P is 0.1 A.
(c) The potential difference across S is 6 V.
(d) The equivalent resistance of the network between A and C is 22.5 Ω.
(e) The potential of B is higher than that of D.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Balanced Wheatstone bridge: P/Q = R/S, no galvanometer current, V_B = V_D
solution.explanation: P/Q = 1/2 = R/S, so the bridge is balanced (a true) and B and D are at the same potential (e false). With no current in the galvanometer, the arms are simply two series pairs across 9 V: P–Q carries 9/30 = 0.3 A (b false) and R–S carries 9/90 = 0.1 A, so V_S = 0.1 × 60 = 6 V (c true). The equivalent resistance is 30 Ω in parallel with 90 Ω, i.e. 22.5 Ω (d true).
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.1 A is the current in the R–S arm, not in P, so (b) is false; at balance B and D are at equal potentials, so (e) is false. Every option except (a), (c) and (d) only includes one of these or leaves out a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Wheatstone bridge

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two cells, X (emf 6.0 V, internal resistance 2.0 Ω) and Y (emf 4.0 V, internal resistance 1.0 Ω), are connected in parallel, positive terminal to positive terminal, and the combination is connected across an external resistor R. The value of R for which no current flows through cell Y is:

solution.concept: A cell carries no current when the p.d. across it equals its emf
solution.explanation: If Y carries no current, the common terminal p.d. equals ε_Y = 4.0 V. Then X alone drives the current through R: (6 − 4)/2 = 1 A, and R = 4 V/1 A.
steps: No current in Y → V = 4.0 V across R
Current from X = (6.0 − 4.0)/2.0 = 1.0 A, all of it through R
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 Ω takes the difference of the emfs (2 V) as the p.d. across R. 1 Ω simply equates R to the internal resistance of Y. 6 Ω uses the current that would circulate between the cells with R removed, (6 − 4)/(2 + 1) A, as the current in R.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells in series and in parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A proton (mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves in a circle at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.2π T (about 0.63 T). The number of revolutions it makes per second is:

solution.concept: Frequency of revolution in a magnetic field: ν = qB/(2πm), independent of speed
solution.explanation: The magnetic force qvB provides the centripetal force mv²/r, so the angular frequency is ω = qB/m and the number of revolutions per second is ω/2π. The speed of the proton is not needed.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.3 × 10⁷ is the angular frequency qB/m (in rad/s), not revolutions per second. 3.2 × 10⁶ drops the π in the field. 5.0 × 10⁶ divides by 4π instead of 2π.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A voltmeter of resistance 1000 Ω has a range of 0–3 V. To use it to measure potential differences up to 15 V, one should connect:

solution.concept: Range of a voltmeter = full-scale current × total resistance
solution.explanation: The full-scale current is 3 V/1000 Ω = 3 mA. To read 15 V at the same current, the total resistance must be 15/0.003 = 5000 Ω, so an extra 4000 Ω is added in series.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5000 Ω is the total resistance needed, not the extra resistance. A resistance in parallel would lower the meter's resistance and draw more current, not extend a voltage range. 15 000 Ω multiplies the meter's resistance by the new range in volts.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the moving coil galvanometer (conversion into voltmeter)
solution.final_answer: Option C: 4000 Ω in series with it

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Two circular loops of wire, of radii R and 2R, lie in the same plane and have a common centre O. The inner loop carries a steady current I. For the magnetic field at O to be zero, the current in the outer loop must be:

options.text: I/2, circulating in the opposite sense

solution.concept: Field at the centre of a circular loop: B = µ₀I/(2R), perpendicular to the plane
solution.explanation: Both fields at O are perpendicular to the common plane. They cancel only if they are equal in magnitude and the currents circulate in opposite senses.
solution.why_others_wrong: Currents in the same sense give fields in the same direction, which add. I/2 inverts the dependence on the radius. 4I takes B ∝ 1/R².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field on the axis of a circular current loop
solution.final_answer: Option D: 2I, circulating in the opposite sense

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A length of wire bent into a single circular turn carries a steady current, and the magnetic field at its centre is B. The same wire is unbent and rewound into a flat coil of two circular turns of equal radius, carrying the same current. The magnetic field at the centre of the coil is now:

solution.concept: B = µ₀NI/(2r) for a flat coil; with a fixed length of wire, r ∝ 1/N
solution.explanation: With two turns from the same length, each turn has half the radius. Doubling N and halving r each double the field.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2B doubles N but forgets that the radius halves. B/2 halves the radius in the wrong direction. B assumes the field depends only on the length of wire.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field on the axis of a circular current loop

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Soft iron is a soft ferromagnetic material: its magnetisation disappears when the external magnetic field is removed.
Statement II: Alnico, an alloy of iron, aluminium, nickel, cobalt and copper, is a hard ferromagnetic material and is used to make permanent magnets.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Hard and soft ferromagnetic materials
solution.explanation: NCERT describes soft ferromagnets, such as soft iron, as materials whose magnetisation disappears on removal of the external field (Statement I true), and hard ferromagnets, such as Alnico, as materials that retain their magnetisation and are used for permanent magnets (Statement II true).
steps: Soft iron: magnetisation lost when field removed → I true
Alnico: retains magnetisation → permanent magnets → II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are NCERT descriptions, so the options that call either of them false are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', ferromagnetism (hard and soft ferromagnets)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
A galvanometer of resistance 100 Ω gives full-scale deflection for a current of 1 mA. Match each instrument to be made from it (List-I) with the resistance needed and its connection (List-II).

List-I:
A. Ammeter of range 0–1 A
B. Ammeter of range 0–10 mA
C. Voltmeter of range 0–1 V
D. Voltmeter of range 0–10 V

List-II:
I. 9900 Ω in series
II. about 0.1 Ω in parallel
III. 900 Ω in series
IV. about 11.1 Ω in parallel

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Shunt S = I_gG/(I − I_g) in parallel for an ammeter; series R = V/I_g − G for a voltmeter
solution.explanation: For an ammeter, the shunt carries the excess current I − I_g at the same p.d. as the galvanometer. For a voltmeter, the total resistance must be V/I_g.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV, B-II gives the larger range the larger shunt, which is the wrong way round. C-I, D-III gives the larger voltage range the smaller series resistance. A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV puts series resistances on the ammeters and shunts on the voltmeters.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the moving coil galvanometer (conversion into ammeter and voltmeter)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A short solenoid of 500 turns, each of cross-sectional area 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m², carries a steady current of 2.0 A. Its length is very small compared with 10 cm, so it behaves like a short bar magnet. Taking µ₀/4π = 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ and ignoring all other magnetic fields, the magnitude of the magnetic field on its axis, 10 cm from its centre, is:

solution.concept: A current-carrying solenoid is equivalent to a bar magnet of moment m = NIA; axial field of a short dipole B = (µ₀/4π)(2m/r³)
solution.explanation: First find the magnetic moment of the solenoid; then use the far-field formula for a point on the axis of a magnetic dipole.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 × 10⁻⁵ T is the equatorial-line value (no factor 2). 4 × 10⁻⁶ T uses 1/r² instead of 1/r³. 8 × 10⁻⁵ T doubles the axial value.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', the bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A paramagnetic sample obeys Curie's law and is far from magnetic saturation. In an applied magnetic field of 0.50 T at a temperature of 300 K, its magnetisation is M. The applied field is raised to 0.80 T and the sample is cooled to 240 K. Its magnetisation becomes:

solution.concept: Curie's law: χ = Cµ₀/T, so M = χH ∝ B₀/T
solution.explanation: The magnetisation is proportional to the applied field and, by Curie's law, inversely proportional to the absolute temperature.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.28 M multiplies by 240/300, as if M increased with temperature. 1.6 M ignores the change of temperature. 1.25 M ignores the change of field.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', paramagnetism (Curie's law)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A moving-coil galvanometer cannot be used as such (without any modification) to measure the current in a circuit.
Reason (R): It gives full-scale deflection for a current of the order of microamperes, and since it must be connected in series, its resistance would change the current being measured.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Why a galvanometer is converted before being used as an ammeter
solution.explanation: NCERT gives exactly these two reasons: the galvanometer is too sensitive (a few µA gives full-scale deflection), and being connected in series its resistance alters the very current it measures. Hence it is converted into an ammeter with a small shunt.
steps: Very sensitive → overloaded by ordinary currents
Series connection + large resistance → changes circuit current
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and R states the reasons why the galvanometer cannot be used directly, so R is the correct explanation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the moving coil galvanometer
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: At points at equal large distances from a short bar magnet, the magnetic field on its axial line points along its magnetic moment, whereas the field on its equatorial line points opposite to its magnetic moment.
Statement II: The magnetic moment of a bar magnet is directed from its north pole to its south pole.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Field of a magnetic dipole: B_axial = (µ₀/4π)(2m/r³), B_equatorial = −(µ₀/4π)(m/r³)
solution.explanation: On the axis the field is 2m/r³ along m; on the equatorial line it is m/r³ directed opposite to m (Statement I true). The magnetic moment of a bar magnet points from its south pole to its north pole (Statement II false).
steps: Axial: along m; equatorial: opposite to m → I true
m points S → N → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II reverses the direction of the magnetic moment; Statement I is the standard dipole result.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', the bar magnet (field of a dipole)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
A magnetic dipole of moment m is held in a uniform magnetic field B, with the angle between m and B as given in List-I. Match each case with the torque τ on the dipole and its potential energy U in List-II.

List-I:
A. 0°
B. 90°
C. 180°
D. 60°

List-II:
I. τ = mB, U = 0
II. τ = 0, U = +mB (unstable equilibrium)
III. τ = (√3/2)mB, U = −mB/2
IV. τ = 0, U = −mB (stable equilibrium)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: τ = mB sin θ; U = −mB cos θ
solution.explanation: The torque vanishes at 0° and 180°, but U is lowest (−mB) at 0°, which is stable, and highest (+mB) at 180°, which is unstable. At 90°, τ is maximum and U = 0. At 60°, τ = mB sin 60° and U = −mB cos 60°.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-II, C-IV swaps the stable and unstable positions. B-III, D-I swaps the 90° and 60° cases. A-I, B-IV gives the parallel position the maximum torque.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', the bar magnet (dipole in a uniform field)
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the examples of magnetic materials given in NCERT are correct?

(a) Oxygen at STP is paramagnetic.
(b) Nitrogen at STP is diamagnetic.
(c) Cobalt is a ferromagnetic substance.
(d) Copper chloride is diamagnetic.
(e) Lead is paramagnetic.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Examples of dia-, para- and ferromagnetic substances
solution.explanation: NCERT lists oxygen (at STP) and copper chloride among paramagnetic substances, nitrogen (at STP) and lead among diamagnetic substances, and iron, cobalt and nickel among ferromagnetic ones. So (a), (b) and (c) are true; copper chloride is paramagnetic (d false) and lead is diamagnetic (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (d) or (e) include a false statement; (a) and (b) only leaves out the true statement (c).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', magnetic properties of materials (examples)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A uniform circular ring of wire of radius R has centre O. A steady current I enters the ring at point A and leaves it at point B, where the radii OA and OB are at right angles, so that the ring is divided into a quarter-circle arc and a three-quarter-circle arc in parallel. The lead wires are straight and lie along the lines OA and OB extended outwards. The magnitude of the magnetic field at O is:

solution.concept: Field at the centre of an arc: B = (µ₀i/2R)(θ/2π); current divides inversely as the resistance (length) of the arcs
solution.explanation: The radial leads point at O and contribute nothing. The quarter arc carries 3I/4 and the three-quarter arc I/4 (currents inversely proportional to arc length). Their fields at O are in opposite directions, and the product i × θ is the same for both arcs, so they cancel.
steps: i₁ = 3I/4 over θ₁ = π/2; i₂ = I/4 over θ₂ = 3π/2
B₁ and B₂ are opposite and equal → B = 0
solution.why_others_wrong: µ₀I/(8R) assumes the current divides equally between the two arcs. 3µ₀I/(32R) counts only the quarter arc. µ₀I/(2R) treats the whole current as going round the complete ring.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field due to a current element, Biot–Savart law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Electrons, starting from rest, are accelerated through a potential difference of 225 V and then enter a uniform magnetic field of 1.0 mT, moving at right angles to it. They move in a circle of radius 5.0 cm. The value of the specific charge e/m of the electron obtained from these data is:

solution.concept: eV = ½mv² and r = mv/(eB) combine to give e/m = 2V/(B²r²)
solution.explanation: The accelerating p.d. fixes the speed; the radius in the magnetic field fixes the momentum per unit charge. Eliminating v gives e/m.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9.0 × 10¹⁰ C/kg drops the factor 2 from ½mv². 1.8 × 10⁸ C/kg does not square B. 9.0 × 10⁹ C/kg does not square r.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Two moving-coil galvanometers G₁ and G₂ have identical radial magnetic fields and identical springs (same torsional constant). G₁ has a coil of 40 turns, each of area 2.0 cm², and resistance 20 Ω; G₂ has a coil of 60 turns, each of area 1.0 cm², and resistance 30 Ω. The ratios of their current sensitivities and of their voltage sensitivities (G₁ : G₂) are, respectively:

solution.concept: Current sensitivity φ/I = NAB/k; voltage sensitivity φ/V = NAB/(kR)
solution.explanation: With the same B and k, the current sensitivity is proportional to NA, and the voltage sensitivity to NA/R.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 : 3 and 8 : 9 multiplies by R instead of dividing for the voltage sensitivity. 2 : 1 and 4 : 3 swaps the two ratios. 3 : 4 and 1 : 2 inverts both.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the moving coil galvanometer (sensitivity)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Two long, ideal, coaxial solenoids are used. The inner one has 1000 turns per metre and carries 2.0 A; the outer one, of larger radius, has 500 turns per metre and carries 3.0 A, its current circulating in the opposite sense to that in the inner solenoid. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnitudes of the magnetic field well inside the inner solenoid and in the region between the two solenoids (away from the ends) are, respectively:

solution.concept: Field of a long ideal solenoid: µ₀nI inside, zero outside; superposition
solution.explanation: Inside the inner solenoid both solenoids contribute, and their fields are opposite. Between the solenoids, the point is outside the inner solenoid (zero field from it) but inside the outer one.
steps: Inside inner: B = µ₀(n₁I₁ − n₂I₂) = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × (2000 − 1500) ≈ 6.3 × 10⁻⁴ T
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.4 × 10⁻³ T adds the two fields although the currents are in opposite senses. 2.5 × 10⁻³ T uses the inner solenoid's field in the region outside it. Zero ignores the outer solenoid, whose field fills the whole region within it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the solenoid

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A plane loop carrying a steady current, placed in a non-uniform magnetic field, can experience a net force.
Statement II: For a plane current loop in a uniform magnetic field, the torque depends on the shape of the loop, not merely on its current, its area and its orientation relative to the field.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Net force on a current loop is zero only in a uniform field; τ = m × B with m = IA
solution.explanation: In a non-uniform field, the forces on different parts of the loop need not cancel, so a net force can act (Statement I true). In a uniform field the torque is m × B, and m = IA depends only on the current and the area (and the direction of the normal), not on the shape (Statement II false).
steps: Non-uniform B: forces on opposite parts unequal → net force possible → I true
Uniform B: τ = IA n̂ × B, shape-independent → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II is false because the magnetic moment of a plane loop is IA for any shape; Statement I is true, so the remaining options are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', torque on current loop, magnetic dipole
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A flat coil of 100 turns, each of area 0.01 m², is in a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T with its plane perpendicular to the field. It is turned through 90°, about a diameter perpendicular to the field, in 0.1 s, so that its plane becomes parallel to the field. The magnitude of the average emf induced in the coil is:

options.text: zero, because the field does not change

solution.concept: Faraday's law: average emf = NΔΦ/Δt
solution.explanation: The flux through each turn falls from BA (plane perpendicular to B) to zero (plane parallel to B). An emf is induced because the flux changes, even though B itself is constant.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 V takes the flux change as 2BA, which is the change for a 180° turn. 0.02 V leaves out the number of turns. Zero ignores that turning the coil changes the flux linked with it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Faraday's law of induction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The reactance of a capacitor is 200 Ω when it is connected to a 50 Hz AC supply. Its reactance when it is connected to a 200 Hz AC supply is:

solution.concept: Capacitive reactance X_C = 1/(2πfC) ∝ 1/f
solution.explanation: The capacitance is unchanged, so the reactance is inversely proportional to the frequency. Raising the frequency four times reduces X_C to one quarter.
solution.why_others_wrong: 800 Ω takes X_C ∝ f, which is the behaviour of an inductor. 100 Ω takes X_C ∝ 1/√f. 200 Ω assumes the reactance does not depend on frequency, which is true only of a resistor.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC voltage applied to a capacitor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A light, closed, horizontal ring of a non-magnetic metal (such as copper) is dropped from rest so that it falls along the vertical axis of a fixed bar magnet whose axis is vertical, and passes right over and beyond it. Neglect air resistance. The acceleration of the ring, both while it is above the magnet and approaching it and after it has passed below the magnet and is moving away from it, is:

options.text: less than g in both stages
less than g while approaching, but greater than g while moving away
equal to g throughout, since no battery is connected to the ring
greater than g while approaching, because the magnet attracts the ring

solution.concept: Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change (the relative motion) that produces it
solution.explanation: While the ring approaches, the flux through it increases and the induced current makes the ring repel the magnet. While it moves away, the flux decreases and the induced current makes the ring attract the magnet. In both stages the magnetic force on the ring is upward, opposing its motion, so its acceleration is less than g.
steps: Approaching: flux increasing → repulsion → upward force
Receding: flux decreasing → attraction → upward force
solution.why_others_wrong: While moving away the induced current attracts the ring back towards the magnet (upward), so a > g is wrong. A battery is not needed: the changing flux itself drives a current. An uncharged, non-magnetic ring is not attracted by a magnet merely because it approaches it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Lenz's law and conservation of energy
solution.final_answer: Option A: less than g in both stages

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The mutual inductance of two coils increases when both are wound on a common soft-iron core.
Statement II: The mutual inductance of two coils depends on their separation and on their relative orientation.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Factors on which mutual inductance depends
solution.explanation: Mutual inductance depends on the geometry of the two coils, their separation and relative orientation, and on the permeability of the medium. A soft-iron core (very large relative permeability) increases the flux linked with the second coil for a given current in the first, so M increases (Statement I true). Moving the coils apart or turning one relative to the other changes the flux linkage and hence M (Statement II true).
steps: Soft-iron core: µ_r ≫ 1 → larger flux linkage → larger M → I true
Separation and orientation change the flux linkage → M changes → II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, so the options that call either of them false are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', inductance (mutual inductance)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A series LCR circuit with R = 100 Ω is connected to a 200 V (rms) AC source and is in resonance; at the source frequency the inductive and capacitive reactances are each 100 Ω. The capacitor is now short-circuited by a wire, everything else unchanged. The rms current and the average power drawn from the source become:

solution.concept: Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²); average power P = I²R = V I cos φ
solution.explanation: At resonance the current was 200/100 = 2 A. With the capacitor shorted, the circuit is R and L only: Z = √(100² + 100²) = 100√2 Ω.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 A and 400 W are the resonance values, before the change. 1 A and 100 W adds R and X_L arithmetically (200 Ω). 283 W multiplies V by I and ignores the power factor 1/√2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', LCR series circuit; power in AC circuit
solution.final_answer: Option C: about 1.41 A and 200 W

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A resistor of 60 Ω, an inductor of reactance 120 Ω and a capacitor of reactance 40 Ω are connected in series to a 200 V (rms) AC supply. Match each pair of points in List-I with the rms voltage between them in List-II.

List-I:
A. Across the resistor
B. Across the inductor
C. Across the capacitor
D. Across the inductor and capacitor taken together

List-II:
I. 160 V
II. 120 V
III. 80 V
IV. 240 V

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Series AC circuit: same current; V_L and V_C are in antiphase, so V_LC = I|X_L − X_C|
solution.explanation: First find the impedance and the current; each voltage is I times the corresponding reactance or resistance. The voltages across L and C are opposite in phase, so across both together they subtract.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-I, D-II swaps V_R and V_LC. B-III, C-IV swaps the inductor and the capacitor. C-I, D-III gives the capacitor the voltage of the L–C pair.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', LCR series circuit (phasor diagram)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A metal wheel has 8 metal spokes, each 0.50 m long, joining its axle to its rim. It rotates at 120 revolutions per minute in a uniform magnetic field of 0.40 T directed parallel to its axle. The emf induced between the axle and the rim is about:

solution.concept: Emf across a rod rotating about one end in a perpendicular field: ε = ½Bωl²; identical spokes are in parallel
solution.explanation: Each spoke is a rod rotating about one end, with the axle end and the rim end common to all spokes. The spokes are therefore in parallel, so the emf between axle and rim is that of one spoke.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.0 V adds the emfs of the 8 spokes as if they were in series. 1.26 V leaves out the factor ½. 0.10 V uses 2 rev/s as if it were the angular speed in rad/s.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', motional electromotive force

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A moving-coil (DC) ammeter connected in a circuit carrying a 50 Hz sinusoidal alternating current shows practically zero reading.
Reason (R): The average value of a sinusoidal alternating current over a complete cycle is zero.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Average and rms values of AC; why AC meters are based on the heating effect
solution.explanation: The deflecting torque on the coil of a moving-coil meter is proportional to the instantaneous current. With a 50 Hz current this torque reverses a hundred times a second and averages to zero over each cycle, so the pointer stays practically at zero. R states the reason.
steps: Torque ∝ i, which reverses every half cycle
Average of i over a cycle = 0 → average torque = 0
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and the zero average value of the current over a cycle is exactly why a moving-coil meter reads zero; AC meters therefore use the heating effect (∝ i²) and read rms values.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC voltage applied to a resistor (rms value)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A closed plane conducting loop is in a region of uniform magnetic field B. In which of the following cases is an emf induced in the loop?

(a) The loop is moved without rotation, its whole area staying inside the uniform field.
(b) The loop is rotated about an axis that lies in its plane and is perpendicular to B.
(c) The loop, with its plane perpendicular to B, is squeezed so that its area decreases.
(d) The loop, with its plane perpendicular to B, is rotated in its own plane about an axis through its centre parallel to B.
(e) The magnitude of B is changed with time, the loop being held fixed with its plane perpendicular to B.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: An emf is induced only when the magnetic flux BA cos θ through the loop changes
solution.explanation: Flux = BA cos θ. (a) B, A and θ are all unchanged → no emf. (b) θ changes → emf. (c) A changes → emf. (d) the loop turns in its own plane, so B, A and θ are unchanged → no emf. (e) B changes → emf.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (a) or (d) include a case of constant flux; (b) and (c) only leaves out case (e).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', magnetic flux; Faraday's law of induction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A series LCR circuit with R = 50 Ω is connected to a 200 V (rms) AC source whose frequency can be varied. The average power drawn from the source at the resonant frequency, and at a frequency for which X_L − X_C = 50 Ω, are, respectively:

solution.concept: Average power P = I²_rms R with I_rms = V_rms/Z
solution.explanation: At resonance Z = R. When the net reactance equals R, Z = R√2, so the current falls by √2 and the power, which goes as I², halves.
solution.why_others_wrong: 800 W and 566 W divides the power, instead of the current, by √2. 400 W and 200 W treats 200 V as a peak value. 800 W and 200 W adds R and X arithmetically (Z = 100 Ω).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', power in AC circuit: the power factor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A long straight wire lies in the plane of a square loop of side 10 cm. Two sides of the loop are parallel to the wire, the nearer one at a distance of 10 cm from it. Taking µ₀/2π = 2 × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the mutual inductance of the wire and the loop is about (ln 2 = 0.693):

solution.concept: M = Φ/I, with the flux of B = µ₀I/(2πx) found by integrating over the loop
solution.explanation: The field of the wire varies as 1/x across the loop, so the flux is found by adding strips of width dx and length a parallel to the wire, from x = 10 cm to x = 20 cm.
steps: Φ = ∫ (µ₀I/2πx) a dx from 0.10 to 0.20 m = (µ₀Ia/2π) ln 2
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ H takes the field at the nearer side as uniform over the loop. 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ H takes the field at the farther side as uniform. 6.9 × 10⁻⁹ H uses µ₀/4π in place of µ₀/2π.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', inductance (mutual inductance)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The coil of an AC generator has 50 turns, each of area 0.020 m², and rotates at an angular speed of 100 rad/s about an axis perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T. The coil (of negligible resistance) is connected across a 25 Ω resistor. The average power dissipated in the resistor is:

solution.concept: Peak emf ε₀ = NBAω; average power in a resistor P = ε_rms²/R = ε₀²/(2R)
solution.explanation: The generator gives a sinusoidal emf of peak value NBAω. The average power uses the rms value, ε₀/√2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 100 W uses the peak emf as if it were the rms value. 25 W divides by 4R. 71 W multiplies the rms emf by the peak current.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC generator; power in AC circuit

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When the switch in a DC circuit containing a coil of large self-inductance is suddenly opened, a spark may jump across the switch contacts.
Reason (R): The rapid decrease of the current induces a large emf in the coil, which opposes the decrease and tends to keep the current flowing.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Self-induced emf ε = −L dI/dt
solution.explanation: Opening the switch makes the current fall almost to zero in a very short time, so dI/dt is very large and so is the self-induced emf L|dI/dt|. This emf acts to maintain the current, and it can be large enough to break down the air between the separating contacts, producing a spark. R explains A.
steps: ε = L|dI/dt| very large, opposing the fall of current
Large emf across the gap → spark; R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and the large self-induced emf from the rapid fall of current is the cause of the spark, so R is the correct explanation of A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', inductance (self-inductance)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A microwave oven uses electromagnetic waves of frequency 2.45 GHz. Taking c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the wavelength of these waves in air is about:

solution.concept: c = fλ for electromagnetic waves
solution.explanation: The wavelength is the speed of light divided by the frequency; 2.45 GHz = 2.45 × 10⁹ Hz.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.2 cm and 1.2 m are off by a factor of ten in the power of ten. 7.4 × 10¹⁷ m multiplies c by f instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic spectrum (microwaves)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Welders wear special glass goggles, or face masks with glass windows, while welding. According to NCERT, these mainly protect their eyes from the large amount of:

options.text: X-rays produced by the welding arc
ultraviolet radiation produced by the welding arc
microwaves produced by the welding arc
radio waves produced by the welding arc

solution.concept: Ultraviolet rays: sources and hazards; ordinary glass absorbs UV
solution.explanation: Welding arcs emit a large amount of ultraviolet radiation, which can damage the eyes. Glass absorbs much of the UV, so welders use glass goggles or masks with glass windows.
steps: Glass absorbs UV → protects the eyes
solution.why_others_wrong: Welding arcs are not significant sources of X-rays, microwaves or radio waves, and glass windows would not be the means of protection against them.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic spectrum (ultraviolet rays)
solution.final_answer: Option B: ultraviolet radiation produced by the welding arc

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the electromagnetic spectrum, as given in NCERT, are correct?

(a) The FM radio band extends from 88 MHz to 108 MHz.
(b) Some snakes can detect ultraviolet waves.
(c) Cellular phones use radio waves in the ultrahigh frequency (UHF) band to transmit voice communication.
(d) Television waves have lower frequencies than the waves of the AM radio band.
(e) Infrared detectors are used in Earth satellites, for example to observe the growth of crops.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared and their uses
solution.explanation: FM: 88–108 MHz (a true). Snakes detect infrared, not ultraviolet; it is many insects whose 'visible' range extends into the ultraviolet (b false). Cellular phones use the UHF band (c true). TV waves (54–890 MHz) have higher frequencies than the AM band (530–1710 kHz) (d false). Infrared detectors are used in Earth satellites, for military purposes and to observe the growth of crops (e true).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (b) or (d) include a false statement; (a) and (c) only leaves out the true statement (e).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic spectrum

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A parallel-plate capacitor has circular plates of radius 4.0 cm and is being charged by a steady current of 1.0 A. Neglect edge effects, so that the changing electric field is confined to the region between the plates. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnitude of the magnetic field at a point midway between the planes of the plates, 8.0 cm from their common axis (outside the edge of the plates), is:

options.text: zero, since no conduction current flows there

solution.concept: Ampere–Maxwell law: ∮B·dl = µ₀(i_c + i_d); between the plates i_d equals the charging current
solution.explanation: A circle of radius 8.0 cm about the axis, in the midplane, encloses the whole region of changing electric field, so the displacement current through it equals the full charging current, 1.0 A.
steps: B × 2πr = µ₀ i_d with i_d = 1.0 A
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ T applies the inside-the-plates result µ₀ir/(2πR²) at a point outside the plates. Zero ignores the displacement current. 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ T uses the plate radius instead of the distance of the point.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', displacement current

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The electric field of a plane electromagnetic wave travelling through a transparent, non-magnetic medium is E = E₀ sin(kx − ωt), with k = 1.5 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ and ω = 3.0 × 10¹⁵ rad s⁻¹. Taking c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the refractive index of the medium and the wavelength of this radiation in vacuum are, respectively:

solution.concept: Wave speed v = ω/k; n = c/v; vacuum wavelength λ₀ = 2πc/ω (the frequency does not change)
solution.explanation: The speed in the medium is ω/k. The frequency is the same in vacuum and in the medium, so the vacuum wavelength follows from ω and c.
solution.why_others_wrong: 419 nm (= 2π/k) is the wavelength inside the medium, not in vacuum. 0.67 is v/c, the reciprocal of the refractive index. 100 nm leaves out the factor 2π.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic waves (nature)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For the same energy of light falling normally on a surface, the momentum delivered to a perfectly reflecting surface is equal to the momentum delivered to a perfectly absorbing surface.
Reason (R): Electromagnetic waves carry momentum; when the total energy U of light is completely absorbed by a surface, the momentum delivered to the surface is U/c.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Momentum carried by electromagnetic waves; momentum transfer on absorption and on reflection
solution.explanation: R is the NCERT result for complete absorption. On perfect reflection the light's momentum is reversed, so its change of momentum, and hence the momentum delivered to the surface, is 2U/c, twice the absorbed value. So A is false.
steps: Absorption: Δp of light = U/c → momentum delivered U/c (R true)
Reflection: momentum reversed → Δp = 2U/c → A false
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false because a reflecting surface receives twice the momentum; R is a correct statement from NCERT.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic waves (momentum and radiation pressure)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ray of light passes through a glass prism of refracting angle 60°. The angle of incidence on the first face is 50° and the angle of emergence from the second face is 40°. The angle of deviation of the ray is:

solution.concept: Deviation by a prism: δ = i + e − A
solution.explanation: The total deviation is the sum of the deviations at the two faces, (i − r₁) + (e − r₂), and r₁ + r₂ = A.
steps: δ = (i − r₁) + (e − r₂) = i + e − (r₁ + r₂)
solution.why_others_wrong: 90° adds i and e but forgets to subtract A. 10° subtracts e from i. 150° adds A instead of subtracting it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction through a prism

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the slits are 0.50 mm apart and light of wavelength 600 nm is used. The angular separation between two consecutive bright fringes, as seen from the slits, is:

solution.concept: Angular fringe width θ = λ/d (small angles)
solution.explanation: Consecutive bright fringes are at angles differing by λ/d, independent of the screen distance.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ rad takes the slit separation as 0.50 m. 8.3 × 10² rad inverts the ratio (d/λ). 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ rad uses λ/2d, the separation between a bright fringe and the next dark fringe.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', interference of light waves and Young's experiment

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Because of the refraction of sunlight by the Earth's atmosphere, the Sun is seen:

options.text: only from a little after the actual sunrise until a little before the actual sunset
about 2 hours before the actual sunrise and until about 2 hours after the actual sunset
at exactly the actual times of sunrise and sunset, since refraction does not change the direction of sunlight
a little before the actual sunrise and until a little after the actual sunset, the time difference at sunset being about 2 minutes

solution.concept: Atmospheric refraction: light bends towards the normal as it enters denser layers of air
solution.explanation: Light from the Sun just below the horizon is bent towards the Earth on passing through the atmosphere, so the Sun appears above the horizon before it actually rises and remains visible after it actually sets. NCERT gives the time difference between actual and apparent sunset as about 2 minutes.
steps: Atmosphere denser near the ground → rays bend towards the Earth
Sun below the horizon still seen → early sunrise, late sunset (about 2 min)
solution.why_others_wrong: Refraction makes the visible day longer, not shorter. The effect is about 2 minutes, not 2 hours. Refraction does change the direction of the light passing through layers of different density.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction
solution.final_answer: Option D: a little before the actual sunrise and until a little after the actual sunset, the time difference at sunset being about 2 minutes

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A convex mirror of radius of curvature 2.0 m is used as a rear-view mirror. A car 1.5 m high is 9.0 m behind the mirror, on its principal axis. The height of the image of the car and its orientation are:

solution.concept: Mirror equation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f and m = −v/u, with f = +R/2 for a convex mirror
solution.explanation: With the Cartesian sign convention, u = −9.0 m and f = +1.0 m. The image is virtual (behind the mirror), erect and diminished.
solution.why_others_wrong: A convex mirror's image of a real object is always erect, so 'inverted' is wrong. About 0.19 m comes from a sign error, taking u = +9.0 m, which gives v = 1.125 m. 1.5 m treats the mirror as plane.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', reflection of light by spherical mirrors (mirror equation)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin equiconvex lens of focal length f is cut into two identical halves by a plane that contains its principal axis. The focal length of each half, for light passing through it, is:

options.text: f, the same as that of the original lens

solution.concept: Lens maker's formula: 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)
solution.explanation: Cutting along the principal axis does not change the material or the curvature of either surface; each half still has the radii R₁ and R₂, so its focal length is unchanged. Only the aperture (and so the amount of light collected) is halved.
steps: Each half keeps both curved surfaces with the same radii
solution.why_others_wrong: 2f is the result for a cut perpendicular to the axis (each half then has one flat surface). f/2 would need more curvature, not less. A half lens still has curved surfaces, so it still converges light.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction by a lens (lens maker's formula)
solution.final_answer: Option C: f, the same as that of the original lens

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A small object is placed on the principal axis of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm, at the distance from the mirror given in List-I. Match each case with the position of the image in List-II.

List-I:
A. 15 cm
B. 20 cm
C. 30 cm
D. 5 cm

List-II:
I. 10 cm behind the mirror (virtual)
II. 30 cm in front of the mirror (real)
III. 15 cm in front of the mirror (real)
IV. 20 cm in front of the mirror (real)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Mirror equation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with f = −10 cm
solution.explanation: Use u negative for real objects. An object between F and C gives an image beyond C; at C, the image is at C; beyond C, the image lies between F and C; inside F, the image is virtual, behind the mirror.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-III, C-II swaps the object and image distances of a conjugate pair. B-I, D-IV gives the object at C a virtual image. C-I, D-III gives the object inside F a real image.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', reflection of light by spherical mirrors (mirror equation)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A concave mirror forms a real image twice the size of an object placed on its principal axis. When the object is moved 5 cm farther away from the mirror, the real image becomes the same size as the object. The focal length of the mirror is:

solution.concept: Concave mirror, real image: |m| = F/(x − F), with x and F the magnitudes of the object distance and focal length
solution.explanation: For a real image, |m| = F/(x − F), where F is the magnitude of the focal length. Write this for both positions and use the 5 cm shift.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 cm equates the shift to the focal length. 15 cm is the first object distance (1.5F). 20 cm is the second object distance, the centre of curvature (2F).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', reflection of light by spherical mirrors (magnification)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A point object in air is 20 cm in front of a concave spherical surface of a large block of glass (refractive index 1.5); the radius of curvature of the surface is 10 cm and the object lies on its axis. The image formed by refraction at this surface is:

options.text: 15 cm from the surface, on the same side as the object (virtual)
10 cm from the surface, on the same side as the object (virtual)

solution.concept: Refraction at a spherical surface: n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R
solution.explanation: With light travelling from air into glass, u = −20 cm. The surface is concave towards the object, so its centre of curvature is on the object side: R = −10 cm.
steps: Negative v: image 15 cm from the surface on the object side, virtual
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 cm inside the glass reverses the sign of v. 'At infinity' results from taking R = +10 cm. 10 cm drops the factor n₂ = 1.5 from n₂/v.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction at spherical surfaces
solution.final_answer: Option A: 15 cm from the surface, on the same side as the object (virtual)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Two thin lenses with the powers given in List-I are placed in contact, coaxially. Match each combination with the focal length of the combination in List-II.

List-I:
A. +2 D and +3 D
B. +5 D and −3 D
C. +4 D and −6 D
D. +2.5 D and +1.5 D

List-II:
I. −50 cm
II. +20 cm
III. +25 cm
IV. +50 cm

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Thin lenses in contact: P = P₁ + P₂; f (in m) = 1/P
solution.explanation: Add the powers with their signs, then f = 100/P cm.
solution.why_others_wrong: B-I, C-IV swaps the signs of the converging and diverging combinations. A-III, D-II swaps two converging combinations. C-III, D-I gives the diverging combination a positive focal length.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', power of a lens; combination of thin lenses in contact
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin glass prism of refracting angle 6° is made of glass of refractive index 1.5. When the prism is completely immersed in water of refractive index 4/3, the deviation it produces in a ray passing through it at near-normal incidence is:

solution.concept: Thin prism: δ = (n − 1)A, with n the refractive index of the prism relative to the surrounding medium
solution.explanation: In water, the relevant refractive index is that of glass relative to water: 1.5/(4/3) = 9/8.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3° is the deviation in air. 1° subtracts the two refractive indices instead of dividing them. 2° uses the refractive index of water in place of that of the glass.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction through a prism

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A flat glass plate (refractive index 1.5) is immersed in water (refractive index 4/3). Unpolarised light travelling in the water falls on the plate. The angle of incidence for which the light reflected from the plate is completely plane polarised is about:

solution.concept: Brewster's law: tan i_B = n₂/n₁ (refractive index of the second medium relative to the first)
solution.explanation: The light goes from water into glass, so the relative refractive index is n_glass/n_water.
solution.why_others_wrong: 56.3° is Brewster's angle for glass in air (tan⁻¹ 1.5). 53.1° is that for water in air (tan⁻¹ 4/3). 41.6° is the angle of refraction at the Brewster angle (90° − i_B).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', polarisation (Brewster's law)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ray of light travelling in glass (refractive index 1.5) strikes a plane glass–water boundary (refractive index of water 4/3) at an angle of incidence of 60°. Which statement correctly describes what happens?

options.text: The ray is totally internally reflected
The ray is refracted into the water, making an angle of about 77° with the normal
The ray is refracted into the water, making an angle of about 50° with the normal
The ray just grazes along the boundary (angle of refraction 90°)

solution.concept: Total internal reflection needs i > C, where sin C = n₂/n₁; otherwise Snell's law gives the refracted ray
solution.explanation: For glass to water, sin C = (4/3)/1.5 = 8/9, so C ≈ 62.7°. The angle of incidence (60°) is smaller than C, so the ray is refracted, bending away from the normal.
solution.why_others_wrong: Total internal reflection would need an angle of incidence above 62.7°; 60° would be enough only at a glass–air boundary (C ≈ 41.8°). About 50° applies Snell's law the wrong way round (bending towards the normal). Grazing emergence occurs only at exactly the critical angle.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', total internal reflection
solution.final_answer: Option B: The ray is refracted into the water, making an angle of about 77° with the normal

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A concave mirror is used as a shaving mirror.
Reason (R): The focal length of a spherical mirror of small aperture is half its radius of curvature.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Uses of concave mirrors; f = R/2
solution.explanation: A concave mirror is used for shaving because, with the face held between the pole and the focus, it forms an erect, magnified, virtual image. R is a true relation for spherical mirrors, but it does not say why the mirror gives an enlarged erect image; it holds equally for convex mirrors, which are useless for shaving.
steps: A: true (erect magnified image when the face is within F)
solution.why_others_wrong: A and R are both true, but R is a general property of all spherical mirrors and does not account for the magnified erect image that makes a concave mirror suitable for shaving.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', reflection of light by spherical mirrors
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about reflecting telescopes, as described in NCERT, are correct?

(a) A mirror objective has no chromatic aberration.
(b) If the reflecting surface of the objective is parabolic, spherical aberration is also removed.
(c) A mirror objective weighs much less than a lens of equivalent optical quality and can be supported over its entire back surface.
(d) The objective of a reflecting telescope is a convex mirror.
(e) Very large lens objectives are easier to make and to support than mirror objectives of the same size.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Advantages of reflecting telescopes
solution.explanation: NCERT lists three advantages of mirror objectives: no chromatic aberration (a), no spherical aberration with a parabolic surface (b), and easier mechanical support since a mirror is lighter and can be supported over its whole back (c). The objective is a concave mirror (d false), and large lenses are heavy, hard to make and can be supported only at the rim (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) or (e) contain a false statement; (a) and (b) only leaves out the true statement (c).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', optical instruments (telescope)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In the diffraction pattern of a single slit illuminated normally, the central maximum lies at θ = 0, the direction in which the waves from all parts of the slit arrive in phase.
Statement II: Increasing the distance of the screen from the slit increases the angular width of the central maximum.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Single-slit diffraction: central maximum at θ = 0; angular width 2λ/a
solution.explanation: At θ = 0 all points of the slit are equidistant (in the far field) from the screen point, so their contributions are in phase and the intensity is maximum (Statement I true). The angular width 2λ/a depends only on λ and the slit width; moving the screen changes the linear width (2λD/a) but not the angular width (Statement II false).
steps: θ = 0: all wavelets in phase → central maximum → I true
Angular width = 2λ/a, independent of D → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II confuses the angular width with the linear width on the screen; Statement I is correct, so the remaining options are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', diffraction (the single slit)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 6.25 cm. It is focused on a distant object so that the final image is formed at the least distance of distinct vision, 25 cm from the eyepiece. The distance between the objective and the eyepiece is:

solution.concept: The objective forms the image of a distant object at its focus; the eyepiece then acts as a magnifier with the final image at D
solution.explanation: The intermediate image is at the focus of the objective (100 cm from it). For the eyepiece, this image is the object, placed so that the final virtual image is 25 cm away.
solution.why_others_wrong: 106.25 cm is the separation in normal adjustment (final image at infinity). 125 cm adds D to f_o. 95 cm subtracts the eyepiece object distance instead of adding it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', optical instruments (refracting telescope)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the slits are 1.0 mm apart and the screen is 1.0 m away. The slits are illuminated by light containing two wavelengths, 600 nm and 400 nm. The least distance from the central maximum at which a bright fringe of the 600 nm light falls exactly on a dark fringe of the 400 nm light is:

solution.concept: Bright fringes at y = nλD/d; dark fringes at y = (m − ½)λD/d
